newsitem.title: UK: Europe biotech booms, jobs up 50 pct - conference.
newsitem.headline: Europe biotech booms, jobs up 50 pct - conference.

text.p: The biotechnology industry is booming across Europe, with employment up 50 percent and 15 percent annual growth, industry experts said on Thursday.
"It's buzzing right now," Bill Pike, biotechnology partner at consultants Ernst and Young, who sponsored an industry conference here, said.

Pike said employee numbers were up by 50 percent. "That means something like 7,000 plus for the U.K. and 25,000 for Europe," he said. That compared to between 150,000 and 200,000 in the United States.

"For Europe as a whole the revenues tend to be up by 20 percent or so," Pike added. Revenues for 1996 were 1.15 billion ecus ($1.3 billion), research and development expense was up 605 million ecus and there were 584 companies. All of these, he predicted, would grow by 20 percent in 1997.

Britain tended to invest in healthcare-oriented companies, like the United States, while continental Europe was skewed towards agricultural biotechnology, Pike added, previewing the company's 1997 biotech survey to be published next month.
Sir William Stewart, President of the Bioindustry Association, said the industry was being transformed as private companies took over more and more of the research.
"The pace of technological change is breathtaking," he said. But, he added: "The culture is changing."
Academic research would no longer be funded by the public pocket unless it could be seen to provide benefit.
For example, Stewart said, the University of Edinburgh's new centre for protein technology was 50 percent funded by the government, and 50 percent by private contracts.
The best university research facilities would be eagerly sought by companies that could not invest in the sophisticated equipment and trained staff, he said.
Stewart predicted another change. With mega-mergers gathering pace in the sectors, big companies would seek to avoid risk and would send marginal research into spinoff companies.
"The spinoff companies will be hungrier -- they will have a greater chance of success," he said.
Anyone seeking to make a profit in biotechnology would have to get in quickly, Stewart advised.
"This is an age of genomics," he said. But as genes and their functions were being discovered, processes involving them were being patented quickly.
"Thos who get in first have claims on genes of unknown function," he said. These could offer up useful peptides and proteins in the future.
Last week consultants Arthur Andersen said Britain's biotech sector would grow dramatically, with the possibility that revenues could double to 1.5 billion stg ($2.4 billion) over the next two years.
